record_type_quote: In 5 experiments, we tested Linkenauger et al.’s claim that right-handed observers overestimate the grasping capacity of their right hand relative to their left hand, and that this, in turn, leads them to underestimate the size of objects to-be-grasped in their right hand relative to their left hand.

targets.authors: Linkenauger S. A., Witt J. K., Bakdash J. Z., Stefanucci J. K., & Proffitt D. R.
targets.title: Asymmetrical body perception: A possible role for neural body representations.
targets.evidence_quote: To test the robustness of the claim that right handers perceive their right hand as bigger than their left hand, in Experiment 1 we asked participants which of their hands was bigger.
targets.outcome_quote: Thus right handers were more likely to say their right hand was larger than their left hand than vice versa. This supports the claim made by Linkenauger et al. (2009) that most right-handed observers perceive their right hand as larger than their left hand.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The dedicated test of the published hand asymmetry finding supports it; later experiments also examine grasping asymmetry.

targets.authors: Linkenauger S. A., Witt J. K., & Proffitt D. R.
targets.title: Taking a hands-on approach: Apparent grasping ability scales the perception of object size.
targets.evidence_quote: We focused on the claim made by Linkenauger et al. (2011) that right-handed observers estimate the size of objects they intend to grasp in their right hand as smaller than objects they intend to grasp in their left hand because they perceive the grasping capacity of their right hand as greater than that of their left hand.
targets.outcome_quote: Thus we did not replicate the results of Linkenauger et al. (2011) because we failed to find the predicted influence of perceived action capacity on spatial perception.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Explicit overall nonreplication verdict for the focal object size finding; successful preliminary hand asymmetry checks do not override it.

reasoning: Identity verified against title, authors and DOI in full article. Two independently published originals are directly retested. Other cited action-specific studies, including Linkenauger et al. 2010, are background rather than separately targeted findings.
